subject: chemistry

items.q: Using the electronegativities Na 0.9, Mg 1.3, Al 1.6, Si 1.9, P 2.2 and Cl 3.2, the electronegativity differences for NaCl, MgCl₂, AlCl₃, SiCl₄ and PCl₃ are 2.3, 1.9, 1.6, 1.3 and 1.0. Which statement about the bonding in this series is correct?
items.correct: Ionic character decreases and covalent character increases gradually along the series.
items.misconception: The bonds are ionic up to AlCl₃ and covalent from SiCl₄ on, where the metals end.
items.why: The metal/non-metal rule is taught early as a quick way to classify compounds, and most examples met at that stage (NaCl, MgO, CO₂, H₂O) obey it, so the rule is taken as a definition rather than as a rough guide. Position in the bonding triangle is set by electronegativity values, not by the element's class. With Sn 2.0 and Cl 3.2, SnCl₄ has Δχ = 1.2, lower than that of SiO₂ (1.5), and it is a molecular liquid. Across the period 3 chlorides Δχ falls gradually from 2.3 (NaCl) to 1.0 (PCl₃), so the bonding changes by degrees.
items.specStatementText: Bonding is best described as a continuum between the ionic, covalent and metallic models, and can be represented by a bonding triangle.
items.random_wrong: Ionic character increases along the series, as the average electronegativity rises.

items.q: Magnesium oxide (χ: Mg 1.3, O 3.4; Δχ = 2.1) lies high in the bonding triangle, towards the ionic vertex. Solid magnesium oxide does not conduct electricity, but molten magnesium oxide does. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Its ions cannot move in the solid, but in the melt they move and carry the current.
items.misconception: Melting splits its MgO molecules into separate ions, which then carry the current.
items.why: Formulae such as NaCl and MgO look like molecular formulae, and dot-and-cross diagrams show one pair of atoms transferring electrons. This 'molecular' picture of ionic bonding is widely reported in chemistry-education research. The formula of an ionic compound gives only the ratio of ions. In solid magnesium oxide the ions are already present, held in fixed positions in the lattice; melting does not create ions, it lets the existing ions move.
items.specStatementText: Bonding is best described as a continuum between the ionic, covalent and metallic models, and can be represented by a bonding triangle.
items.random_wrong: Its ions become liquid when it melts, and liquid ions can carry charge but solid ones cannot.

items.q: The position of a binary compound in the bonding triangle is found from the electronegativities of its two elements. In the triangle the metallic vertex is at the bottom left, the covalent vertex at the bottom right and the ionic vertex at the top; the two bottom vertices are elements, for which Δχ = 0. For aluminium chloride, AlCl₃, χ(Al) = 1.6 and χ(Cl) = 3.2. What is the x-coordinate of AlCl₃ in the bonding triangle?
items.why:
Students carry over the procedure for mean values weighted by numbers of particles, used for relative formula mass and relative atomic mass from isotope abundances, and apply it to the formula. The bonding triangle describes the bond between the two elements, so each element is counted once: for AlCl₃ the x-coordinate is (1.6 + 3.2)/2 = 2.4, not 2.8.

Working: The bottom edge (both bottom vertices) has Δχ = 0 and the ionic vertex at the top has the largest Δχ, so Δχ is the vertical (y) coordinate and the horizontal (x) coordinate is the average electronegativity. x = (χ(Al) + χ(Cl))/2 = (1.6 + 3.2)/2 = 2.4 (no units). The y-coordinate, Δχ = 3.2 − 1.6 = 1.6, is not asked.
items.specStatementText: The position of a compound in the bonding triangle is determined by the relative contributions of the three bonding types to the overall bond.
items.working: The bottom edge (both bottom vertices) has Δχ = 0 and the ionic vertex at the top has the largest Δχ, so Δχ is the vertical (y) coordinate and the horizontal (x) coordinate is the average electronegativity. x = (χ(Al) + χ(Cl))/2 = (1.6 + 3.2)/2 = 2.4 (no units). The y-coordinate, Δχ = 3.2 − 1.6 = 1.6, is not asked.

items.q: With χ(Sn) = 2.0 and χ(Cl) = 3.2, tin(IV) chloride, SnCl₄, has an electronegativity difference of 1.2 and an average electronegativity of 2.6. Sodium chloride has an electronegativity difference of 2.3. Which prediction about SnCl₄ is correct?
items.correct: It has a low boiling point, as its molecules are held by weak intermolecular forces.
items.misconception: Its vapour consists of separate Sn and Cl atoms, as boiling must break its Sn–Cl bonds.
items.why: Diagrams show molecules or chains as bonded structures, and 'breaking apart' on melting is read as bond breaking. Confusing covalent bonds with intermolecular forces is among the most widely reported misconceptions in chemistry-education research. In molecular substances and plastics, changes of state and softening overcome only the weak intermolecular forces between molecules or chains. That is why SnCl₄ boils at 114 °C although its Sn–Cl bonds are strong, and why a thermoplastic can be softened and reshaped many times without its chains becoming shorter.
items.specStatementText: The position of a compound in the bonding triangle is determined by the relative contributions of the three bonding types to the overall bond.
items.random_wrong: It has a high melting point, as a metal chloride is a lattice of metal and chloride ions.

items.q: In the bonding triangle, the x-axis is the average electronegativity of the two elements and the y-axis is their electronegativity difference, Δχ. The metallic vertex is at the bottom left (low average, Δχ = 0), the covalent vertex at the bottom right (high average, Δχ = 0) and the ionic vertex at the top. Compound P is formed from two metals with χ = 1.0 and 1.3 (average 1.15, Δχ = 0.3). Carbon disulfide, CS₂, with χ(C) = 2.6 and χ(S) = 2.6, has average 2.6 and Δχ = 0. Which prediction about P does the bonding triangle support?
items.correct: It conducts electricity as a solid, as its valence electrons are delocalized.
items.misconception: It is a molecular substance like CS₂, as its small Δχ means shared electron pairs.
items.why: Before meeting the bonding triangle, students learn a one-dimensional scale running from ionic to polar covalent to non-polar covalent, which has no place for metallic bonding. Two coordinates are needed. With Δχ close to zero, a low average electronegativity (atoms that hold their valence electrons weakly) gives metallic bonding with delocalized electrons, while a high average (atoms that hold electrons strongly) gives covalent bonding with shared pairs. A compound of two metals with χ = 1.0 and 1.3 lies near the metallic vertex; CS₂ (both 2.6) lies on the bottom edge towards the covalent side.
items.specStatementText: The position of a compound in the bonding triangle is determined by the relative contributions of the three bonding types to the overall bond.
items.random_wrong: It conducts when molten but not as a solid, as its unequal χ values mean it has ions.

items.q: Which description of an alloy is correct?
items.correct: A mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals, in variable amounts
items.misconception: A compound of a metal with other elements, bonded in a fixed ratio by formula
items.why: Alloys are made by melting elements together and have properties different from those of the components, which students associate with chemical reactions; the everyday word 'combine' reinforces the idea. An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals. The atoms of the added element sit in the metallic lattice, held by the same non-directional metallic bonding, in any proportion within a range. Its hardness comes from the different-sized atoms disrupting the layers, not from a new compound.
items.specStatementText: Alloys are mixtures of a metal and other metals or non-metals. They have enhanced properties.
items.random_wrong: A mixture of two or more metals, with no atoms of a non-metal present in it

items.q: A bronze used for springs and bearings is an alloy of copper containing about 5% tin. Tin atoms are larger than copper atoms, and pure tin is a soft metal. Which statement comparing this bronze with pure copper is correct?
items.correct: Bronze is harder, as the larger tin atoms disrupt the layers of copper atoms.
items.misconception: Bronze is softer, as a mixture of metals is weaker than a pure metal.
items.why: In everyday language 'pure' implies 'better', and mixing is associated with dilution or weakening. Students also remember that metals are malleable and assume that adding another element makes this even easier. Alloying normally increases hardness and strength. The atoms of the added element are a different size from those of the main metal, so they disrupt the regular layers and the layers cannot slide over each other as easily. Bronze is harder than copper; steel is harder than iron.
items.specStatementText: Alloys are mixtures of a metal and other metals or non-metals. They have enhanced properties.
items.random_wrong: Bronze is softer, as its tin atoms are themselves soft and pass this on to the alloy.

items.q: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Like copper, brass conducts electricity and can be hammered into shape. Which statement about the bonding in brass is correct?
items.correct: Delocalized electrons hold all the cations, as the bonding is non-directional.
items.misconception: Covalent bonds join the atoms, as metallic bonding needs atoms of a single element.
items.why: Metallic bonding is introduced using pure metals such as sodium and copper, and bonding in compounds is taught only as ionic or covalent, so students confine metallic bonding to elements. Metallic bonding is non-directional: the delocalized electrons attract all the cations around them, whatever element each cation comes from. Brass and bronze are held by metallic bonding, which is why they conduct electricity and can be shaped, and a compound of two metals lies near the metallic vertex of the bonding triangle.
items.specStatementText: Alloys are mixtures of a metal and other metals or non-metals. They have enhanced properties.
items.random_wrong: Copper and zinc atoms bond in a fixed ratio, as they would in a compound of the two.

items.q: Which statement about polymers is correct?
items.correct: Cellulose (natural) and nylon (synthetic) are both polymers built from monomers.
items.misconception: Polymers are synthetic plastics; substances made by living things are not.
items.why: In everyday language 'polymer' is used almost only for plastics, and polymers are usually introduced through poly(ethene) and other products of the petrochemical industry. A polymer is any macromolecule built from many repeating monomer units. Cellulose and starch are polymers of glucose, proteins are polymers of amino acids and DNA is a polymer of nucleotides; all are made by living organisms.
items.specStatementText: Polymers are large molecules, or macromolecules, made from repeating subunits called monomers.
items.random_wrong: Fats are natural polymers made of many glycerol and fatty acid units.

items.q: Poly(ethene) is a plastic that softens when heated and can then be moulded into a new shape. What happens in the plastic as it softens?
items.correct: The chains gain enough energy to overcome the forces between them and slide past each other.
items.misconception: Heat flows into the gaps between the chains as a substance and pushes the chains apart.
items.why: Everyday language treats heat as a substance ('let the heat in', 'heat flows', 'keep the heat in'), and diagrams show heat as arrows flowing into objects. Thinking of heat as a substance is widely reported in science-education research on heat and temperature. Heating transfers energy to the chains, so they move more. When they have enough energy to partly overcome the intermolecular forces between them, they slide past each other and the plastic softens. Nothing material is added, and the mass of the plastic does not change.
items.specStatementText: Polymers are large molecules, or macromolecules, made from repeating subunits called monomers.
items.random_wrong: The covalent bonds between neighbouring chains break, so the chains separate.

items.q: Which property of poly(ethene) is correctly explained in terms of its structure?
items.correct: It is an electrical insulator, as all of its valence electrons are in localized bonds.
items.misconception: It is an electrical insulator, as it contains no metal atoms to carry a current.
items.why: Students name compounds after their elements and first meet conductivity as a property of metals, so they reason from the elements present rather than from the bonding. Mixtures, which do keep some properties of their components, reinforce the idea. The properties of a compound depend on its bonding and structure. Magnesium oxide contains magnesium but does not conduct as a solid; tin(IV) chloride contains tin but is a molecular liquid; graphite contains no metal but conducts. Conductivity needs mobile charged particles: delocalized electrons or mobile ions.
items.specStatementText: Polymers are large molecules, or macromolecules, made from repeating subunits called monomers.
items.random_wrong: It softens on heating, as the covalent bonds in its chains break apart.

items.q: Propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, forms the addition polymer poly(propene), written as [repeating unit]ₙ. Which option gives the repeating unit and describes it correctly?
items.correct: –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–, one unit of a single long chain
items.misconception: –CH₂=CH(CH₃)–, keeping each monomer's C=C
items.why: The repeating unit is drawn by copying the monomer and adding bonds at the ends, and because the unit contains the same atoms as the monomer, students assume it also has the same bonds. Addition polymerization happens because one bond of each C=C breaks. Each former C=C carbon then forms a new single bond to the next unit, so it still forms four bonds in total. From propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, the repeating unit is –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–, and a chain section can be traced back to its monomer by restoring the C=C.
items.specStatementText: Addition polymers form by the breaking of a double bond in each monomer.
items.random_wrong: –CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–, all three carbons in the main chain

items.q: A section of an addition polymer is –CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–. Which is the monomer?
items.correct: (CH₃)₂C=CH₂
items.misconception: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃
items.why: Students picture polymers as long straight chains and write the carbon atoms of the monomer in a line, as in the formula CH₂=CHCH₃, without asking which carbons were joined by the double bond. Only the C=C carbons take part in the polymerization, so they alone form the main chain; every other group stays attached as a side group. Poly(propene) has CH₃ side groups on alternate carbons: –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–.
items.specStatementText: Addition polymers form by the breaking of a double bond in each monomer.

items.q: Nylon-6,6 forms from hexane-1,6-diamine, H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ (M_r = 116.24), and hexanedioyl dichloride, ClOC(CH₂)₄COCl (M_r = 183.04). Using A_r values H 1.01, C 12.01, N 14.01, O 16.00 and Cl 35.45, what is the M_r of one repeating unit of the polymer?
items.why:
Addition polymerization is usually taught first and becomes the model for 'polymerization' in general; the loss of a small molecule is then forgotten when the monomers do not contain C=C. Condensation polymers form by reaction between functional groups, with a small molecule released at each link. The repeating unit of nylon-6,6 has two HCl (from the diacyl dichloride) or two H₂O (from the diacid) fewer than the two monomers; starch has one H₂O fewer per glucose unit than glucose.

Working: Repeating unit: –NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO– = C₁₂H₂₂N₂O₂. M_r = 12 × 12.01 + 22 × 1.01 + 2 × 14.01 + 2 × 16.00 = 144.12 + 22.22 + 28.02 + 32.00 = 226.36 ≈ 226.4. Check from the monomers: two amide links form per repeating unit, each releasing HCl (M_r = 1.01 + 35.45 = 36.46): 116.24 + 183.04 − 2 × 36.46 = 226.36.
items.specStatementText: Condensation polymers form by the reaction between functional groups in each monomer with the release of a small molecule.
items.working: Repeating unit: –NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO– = C₁₂H₂₂N₂O₂. M_r = 12 × 12.01 + 22 × 1.01 + 2 × 14.01 + 2 × 16.00 = 144.12 + 22.22 + 28.02 + 32.00 = 226.36 ≈ 226.4. Check from the monomers: two amide links form per repeating unit, each releasing HCl (M_r = 1.01 + 35.45 = 36.46): 116.24 + 183.04 − 2 × 36.46 = 226.36.

items.q: Ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH₂CH₂OH, and hexanedioic acid, HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH, react to form a polyester. Which option gives the repeating unit and describes it correctly?
items.correct: –OCH₂CH₂OOC(CH₂)₄CO–, with two H₂O lost per unit
items.misconception: –OCH₂CH₂OOC(CH₂)₄COOH, with one H₂O lost per unit
items.why: A procedural error: students count the links they can see inside the repeating unit and forget the link that joins each unit to the next one in the chain. In a chain of repeating units from a diol and a diacid, every monomer uses both of its functional groups. Each diol and each diacid residue is linked on both sides, so for every repeating unit two ester links form and two H₂O are released: HOCH₂CH₂OH + HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH − 2 H₂O gives –OCH₂CH₂OOC(CH₂)₄CO–.
items.specStatementText: Condensation polymers form by the reaction between functional groups in each monomer with the release of a small molecule.

items.q: Which statement about biological macromolecules is correct?
items.correct: Proteins are hydrolyzed to amino acids, with water used to break each amide link.
items.misconception: Starch forms from glucose by hydrolysis, with a water molecule released at each link.
items.why: Both terms involve water and describe reverse processes, so they are easily swapped; the prefix 'hydro-' is taken to mean that water is produced. 'Hydrolysis' means splitting by water: a water molecule reacts with each link, adding –H to one fragment and –OH to the other. Biological macromolecules form by condensation, with water released, and are broken down by hydrolysis, with water used.
items.specStatementText: Condensation polymers form by the reaction between functional groups in each monomer with the release of a small molecule.
items.random_wrong: DNA is hydrolyzed simply as it dissolves in water, without any covalent bonds breaking.

items.q: Hexane-1,6-diamine, H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂, and decanedioic acid, HOOC(CH₂)₈COOH, react to form the polyamide nylon-6,10. Which option gives the repeating unit and describes it correctly?
items.correct: –NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₈CO–, with two H₂O lost per unit
items.misconception: –NH(CH₂)₆NH–, with a single monomer in each unit
items.why: The rule 'one monomer gives one repeating unit' is learned for addition polymers and then applied to condensation polymers made from two monomers. When two different monomers alternate in the chain, the smallest unit that repeats contains one of each. For nylon-6,6 it is –NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO–, containing the diamine residue and the diacid residue.
items.specStatementText: Condensation polymers form by the reaction between functional groups in each monomer with the release of a small molecule.
items.random_wrong: –NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₈COOH, with one H₂O lost per unit

items.q: If a compound's bonding is intermediate between two bonding types, such as ionic and covalent, are some of its bonds of one type and the others of the other type?
items.correct: No. Each bond has intermediate character; all the equivalent bonds in the compound are alike.
items.misconception: A compound with intermediate bonding contains a mixture of bonds of the pure types: some are fully ionic and the rest are fully covalent (or fully metallic), in proportions given by its percentage character.
items.why: Percentages are usually met as fractions of a population (percentage by mass, percentage of students), so 'partly ionic' is read as 'a proportion of the bonds are ionic'. Students who hold only the separate ionic and covalent models have no picture of a single bond that is in between. Bonding character describes each bond, not a count of bonds. In SiCl₄ all four Si–Cl bonds are equivalent: each is a polar covalent bond with some ionic character. Moving through the bonding triangle changes the character of every bond gradually.
items.specStatementText: Bonding is best described as a continuum between the ionic, covalent and metallic models, and can be represented by a bonding triangle.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do individual atoms, ions or molecules have the bulk properties of the material they make up, such as being hard, soft or liquid?
items.correct: No. Hardness, softness, melting and conductivity are properties of the material, explained by how its particles are arranged and bonded, not properties of single particles.
items.misconception: Individual particles have the properties of the bulk material: atoms of a soft metal are themselves soft, ions melt when a solid melts, and a polymer chain itself softens when a plastic softens.
items.why: Everyday reasoning transfers the properties of a substance to its 'bits', and students first meet particles as tiny pieces of the material. Attributing macroscopic properties to particles is one of the most widely reported misconceptions in chemistry-education research. Bulk properties arise from the arrangement of particles and the forces between them. A material is hard when its layers of particles cannot slide easily, it melts when its particles become free to move past each other, and it softens when the attractions between its particles are weakened. The particles themselves do not melt, soften or harden.
items.specStatementText: Bonding is best described as a continuum between the ionic, covalent and metallic models, and can be represented by a bonding triangle.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the average electronegativity of a binary compound calculated?
items.correct: By adding the two electronegativities and dividing by 2.
items.misconception: The x-coordinate is found by adding the two electronegativities, without dividing by 2.
items.why: A procedural slip: the student starts to calculate the mean but omits the division by 2, a step that is easily dropped in a two-step calculation. The x-coordinate is an average, so for AlCl₃ it is (1.6 + 3.2)/2 = 2.4. A sum such as 4.8 cannot be a coordinate, because no element has an electronegativity above 4.0.
items.specStatementText: The position of a compound in the bonding triangle is determined by the relative contributions of the three bonding types to the overall bond.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the bonding triangle, which coordinate measures ionic character?
items.correct: The electronegativity difference, Δχ, on the y-axis. The average electronegativity on the x-axis decides whether low-Δχ bonding is metallic or covalent; it does not measure ionic character.
items.misconception: The average electronegativity measures ionic character (or the two axes are interchanged), so the higher the average, the more ionic the compound.
items.why: Students link high electronegativity with 'grabbing electrons' and so with ions, and two unfamiliar axes both labelled with electronegativity are easy to interchange. Ionic character rises with Δχ (y-axis, upwards). A high average electronegativity (x-axis, to the right) with a small Δχ means covalent bonding: PCl₃ has a higher average (2.7) than NaCl (2.05) but is much less ionic, because its Δχ is 1.0 against 2.3.
items.specStatementText: The position of a compound in the bonding triangle is determined by the relative contributions of the three bonding types to the overall bond.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does any difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms mean that electrons are transferred and ions form?
items.correct: No. A small Δχ gives a bond with slight polarity; transfer of electrons to form ions is a good model only when Δχ is large.
items.misconception: Whenever the two atoms have different electronegativities, the less electronegative atom gives electrons to the other, so the bond is ionic.
items.why: The partial charges δ+ and δ− on polar bonds are read as the full charges of ions, and students are first taught that metals 'give' electrons to other elements. The confusion of polar covalent with ionic bonding is widely reported. Electronegativity difference shifts shared or delocalized electrons towards one atom; it transfers them completely only in the limit of a large Δχ. With Δχ = 0.3 between two metals the bonding is almost purely metallic; copper (χ 1.9) and zinc (χ 1.7) in brass share delocalized electrons and do not form ions of opposite charge.
items.specStatementText: The position of a compound in the bonding triangle is determined by the relative contributions of the three bonding types to the overall bond.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can an alloy contain a non-metal?
items.correct: Yes. An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals; steel, for example, is iron with a small percentage of carbon.
items.misconception: An alloy is a mixture of metals only; a mixture containing a non-metal is not an alloy.
items.why: Some introductory courses define an alloy as 'a mixture of metals', and the most familiar examples (bronze, brass, solder) contain only metals. The IB definition of an alloy is a mixture of a metal and other metals or non-metals. Steels contain carbon, and stainless steel contains chromium, nickel and a little carbon. The added atoms, metal or non-metal, disrupt the layers of the main metal.
items.specStatementText: Alloys are mixtures of a metal and other metals or non-metals. They have enhanced properties.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are fats polymers?
items.correct: No. A fat (triglyceride) is a single molecule made from one glycerol and three fatty acids; it has no repeating chain of monomer units.
items.misconception: All large biological molecules are polymers, so fats are polymers built from many glycerol and fatty acid units.
items.why: Fats are taught alongside carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids as one of the main groups of biological molecules, and they are built from smaller units, so students assume they are polymers like the others. A polymer has many repeating units. A triglyceride contains exactly one glycerol and three fatty acid units, so it is not a polymer.
items.specStatementText: Polymers are large molecules, or macromolecules, made from repeating subunits called monomers.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is glucose a polymer?
items.correct: No. Glucose is a monomer; starch, glycogen and cellulose are the polymers made from it.
items.misconception: A molecule that is a building block of a natural polymer, such as glucose or an amino acid, is itself a polymer.
items.why: The words 'monomer' and 'polymer' are similar, and glucose and amino acids are met in the same lessons as the polymers made from them, so students attach the label 'polymer' to the whole topic. A monomer is a small molecule; a polymer is a macromolecule made from many monomer units joined together. Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is a monomer; starch contains thousands of glucose units.
items.specStatementText: Polymers are large molecules, or macromolecules, made from repeating subunits called monomers.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the chains in a plastic such as poly(ethene) joined to each other by covalent bonds?
items.correct: No. In poly(ethene) and other thermoplastics the separate chains are held together only by intermolecular forces.
items.misconception: The chains in a plastic are joined to neighbouring chains by covalent bonds, and these bonds between chains break when the plastic is heated.
items.why: Plastics are strong solids, and students picture a solid as held by bonds; diagrams of tangled chains are read as a network of bonded chains. In a thermoplastic such as poly(ethene), covalent bonds hold atoms together only within each chain. Neighbouring chains are attracted by intermolecular forces, which the chains overcome more easily as they gain energy on heating, so the chains slide past each other and the plastic softens without any covalent bonds breaking.
items.specStatementText: Polymers are large molecules, or macromolecules, made from repeating subunits called monomers.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do plastics persist in the environment because they are synthetic?
items.correct: No. Persistence depends on structure: the chains of poly(ethene) are held together by strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds that few microorganisms can break down. Some synthetic polymers, such as poly(lactic acid), are biodegradable.
items.misconception: Only natural substances can be broken down by living things; anything synthetic, because it is man-made, cannot biodegrade.
items.why: Everyday language contrasts 'natural' with 'artificial' or 'chemical', and the plastics met in everyday life are both synthetic and persistent, so the two ideas are merged. Whether a substance biodegrades depends on its bonds and whether organisms have enzymes that can break them. Poly(ethene) persists because its long chains of C–C and C–H bonds are strong and non-polar and are not attacked by water or by the enzymes of microorganisms.
items.specStatementText: Polymers are large molecules, or macromolecules, made from repeating subunits called monomers.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the formula [–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–]ₙ, does n count separate molecules?
items.correct: No. n is the number of repeating units joined in one chain; the formula represents a single long molecule.
items.misconception: The subscript n means that the polymer is n different molecules, each a copy of the repeating unit.
items.why: In most formulae a coefficient or subscript counts separate items (2 H₂O, n mol), and the brackets make the repeating unit look like a separate particle. n counts repeating units covalently bonded together in one chain, usually thousands of them. A polymer sample is a collection of such chains of similar structure and varying length.
items.specStatementText: Addition polymers form by the breaking of a double bond in each monomer.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a small molecule released when an addition polymer forms?
items.correct: No. In addition polymerization the monomers join by opening their C=C bonds and no other product forms; the polymer contains every atom of the monomers.
items.misconception: A small molecule such as water is released each time two monomers join, so addition polymerization also produces water or another small molecule.
items.why: In biology, students learn that large molecules are built from small ones with the loss of water, and this idea is carried over to every reaction in which molecules join. In addition polymerization no other product forms: the repeating unit has exactly the same atoms as the monomer, so the monomer of a chain such as –CH₂–C(CH₃)₂– is CH₂=C(CH₃)₂, with no extra atoms to be lost.
items.specStatementText: Addition polymers form by the breaking of a double bond in each monomer.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the small molecule released in condensation polymerization always water?
items.correct: No. It depends on the functional groups: a carboxylic acid group reacting with an amine or alcohol releases H₂O, but an acyl chloride group (–COCl) releases HCl.
items.misconception: The small molecule released in a condensation reaction is always water, whatever the functional groups.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'condensation' is water forming from vapour, and most condensation reactions met in biology and in esterification release water. The small molecule is made from the atoms removed from the two reacting groups. –COOH + H₂N– gives –CONH– + H₂O, but –COCl + H₂N– gives –CONH– + HCl. With hexanedioyl dichloride, two HCl are released per repeating unit of nylon-6,6.
items.specStatementText: Condensation polymers form by the reaction between functional groups in each monomer with the release of a small molecule.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is hydrolysis the same as dissolving in water?
items.correct: No. Hydrolysis is a chemical reaction in which a bond is broken by reaction with water; dissolving is a physical process in which no covalent bonds break.
items.misconception: Hydrolysis is dissolving in water: the polymer mixes with water and falls apart into its monomers without any bonds being broken.
items.why: Both processes involve water and make a solid 'disappear' into solution, and the everyday phrase 'broken down in water' covers both. Dissolving separates molecules from each other but leaves each molecule intact. Hydrolysis breaks covalent links: in the digestion of a protein, water reacts with each amide (peptide) link to give amino acids, a reaction catalysed by enzymes.

items.q: In molten magnesium oxide, is the electric current carried by electrons?
items.correct: No. In a molten (or aqueous) ionic compound the current is carried by the movement of ions; electrons flow only in the electrodes and external circuit.
items.misconception: In any conductor, including a molten or dissolved ionic compound, the current is carried by electrons moving through it.
items.why: Current is first taught as a flow of electrons in metal wires, so students assume electrons carry the charge in every conductor. The belief that electrons move through electrolytes is widely reported in chemistry-education research on electrical conductivity and electrochemistry. Solid MgO has no mobile charged particles. In the melt, Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions move towards the electrodes of opposite charge, and this movement of ions is the current. MgO has no delocalized electrons in either state.
items.specStatementText: Bonding is best described as a continuum between the ionic, covalent and metallic models, and can be represented by a bonding triangle.
